core: The working definition of adjusting entries: journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to record transactions not yet captured in the books, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting
Why they exist: gradual events such as supplies used, prepaid rent consumed, and wages earned but unpaid produce no source document and no entry during the period (the timing problem, stated simply)
The common types named, each with one line and an original example: prepayments used up, accrued expenses, accrued revenue
When they happen: after the trial balance and before the financial statements (the cycle position; trial-balance and accounting-cycle are sibling topics, referenced only)
Adjusting vs closing: correcting the period's balances vs resetting the accounts for the next period (the distinction)
The honest framing: adjustments are how accountants tell the truth about a period (the reality check)
supporting: The accounting equation must remain equal after adjusting entries (OpenStax Section 4.2)
Each adjusting entry pairs one income statement account with one balance sheet account and never touches cash (CFI; OpenStax Section 4.2)
The revenue recognition and expense recognition (matching) principles and the time period assumption underlie the need for adjustments (OpenStax Sections 4.1 and 4.2)
Estimate-based adjustments such as depreciation exist (CFI), but depreciation mechanics belong to the depreciation sibling topic
outOfScope: The trial balance and what it checks (sibling topic accounting:foundations:trial-balance; referenced only)
The accounting cycle's full step sequence (sibling topic accounting:foundations:accounting-cycle; referenced only)
Accrual accounting versus cash accounting in depth (sibling topic accounting:foundations:accrual-accounting; referenced only)
Depreciation computation and methods (sibling topic accounting:foundations:depreciation; referenced only)
Journal-entry mechanics and debits/credits (sibling topics journal-entries, debits-and-credits; referenced only)
Closing-entry procedure in detail (the adjusting-vs-closing distinction is drawn here; the procedure belongs to the cycle topic)

claims.claim: Adjusting entries update accounting records at the end of a period for any transactions that have not yet been recorded; in this lesson they are defined as journal entries made at period end to record things the books have not yet captured.

Journal entries are usually triggered by an original source document such as an invoice, receipt, or time sheet, and not every event produces one: using supplies from the supply closet generates no document, and a customer does not remind the business that revenue has now been earned.

Adjusting entries are necessary to ensure the income statement and balance sheet present correct, up-to-date numbers; the reasons include the impracticality of recording every daily event (e.g., supplies use), costs that must be recognized at period end (depreciation, rent, insurance), and source documents not yet received (e.g., a utility bill).

The two main families of adjusting entries are deferrals and accruals: deferrals cover prepaid expenses (supplies, insurance, rent — assets whose used portion becomes an expense) and unearned revenues (advance payments that become revenue as the service is provided); accruals cover accrued revenues and accrued expenses.

Accrued revenues are earned in a period but not yet recorded or collected, with examples including interest earned and services completed but not yet billed; accrued expenses are incurred in a period but not yet recorded or paid, with examples including interest, taxes, and salaries.
Each adjusting entry pairs one income statement account (revenue or expense) with one balance sheet account (asset or liability), and adjusting entries do not involve cash.
Just as the accounting equation must be equal, it must remain equal after adjusting entries are made.
In the accounting cycle, adjusting entries come after the unadjusted trial balance and before the adjusted trial balance and the financial statements.

Under accrual accounting, revenues are recognized when earned and expenses when incurred (the revenue recognition and expense recognition or matching principles), regardless of when cash moves; the accounting period can be a month, quarter, half-year, or full year.

Adjusting entries update the period's balances before the statements, while closing entries, made after the statements, zero out revenue and expense accounts and leave balance sheet accounts open, so the next period starts fresh.

The honest framing: adjustments are the routine mechanism that makes the statements reflect reality — OpenStax says they ensure the income statement and balance sheet present correct, up-to-date numbers, and CFI says the financial statements end up reflecting a more accurate financial picture of the company.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the adjustment types are grouped.
positions: OpenStax groups adjusting entries into two families, deferrals and accruals (Section 4.2)
CFI adds a third category of estimate-based entries (depreciation, allowance for doubtful accounts)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the assignment's three-way naming — prepayments used up, accrued expenses, accrued revenue — which covers both families, and notes depreciation as a related adjustment owned by its own sibling lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number of steps in the accounting cycle differs across textbooks.
positions: OpenStax numbers the cycle with nine steps including unadjusted and adjusted trial balances (Section 3.3)
CFI counts eight steps with a separate worksheet step (Accounting Cycle guide)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids step counts and states only the relative position — after the trial balance, before the financial statements — which is consistent across both sources.

sourceRecords.title: Adjusting Journal Entries in Accrual Accounting — Types
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: adjusting entries as the entries that record the associated revenue and expense recognition, with each adjusting journal entry consisting of an income statement account (revenue or expense) and a balance sheet account (asset or liability); the accrual family (accrued revenue: earned with goods/services delivered while cash has neither been received nor recorded, e.g. credit sales; accrued expense: incurred before cash payment, e.g. utility bills, salaries, taxes); the deferral family (deferred revenue as an unearned-revenue liability recognized when goods or services are delivered; prepaid expenses such as prepaid insurance premiums and rent recognized monthly as consumed); estimate-based adjustments (depreciation, allowance for doubtful accounts) as a third category; and the claim that with estimates the financial statements reflect a more accurate financial picture of the company. Page states no explicit license; used REFERENCE_ONLY, facts restated in original prose.
